extracted.intended_audience: literate general public / readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century readers interested in manners, morals, and news)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, moralizing/observational periodical essays and letters offering guidance on social behaviour, education, news selection, and good writing — the style of The Spectator. Includes proposals for news columns and reflections on virtues like modesty and mercy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of speculative observation
rubrics_metrics.description: To be ever unconcerned, and ever looking on new Objects with an endless Curiosity, is a Delight known only to those who are turned for Speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enjoy things as objects of speculation rather than for worldly advantage; keep the mind open to gratification from any object it meets. Practically: rise early, rove about town, observe varied scenes (markets, coffee-houses, Exchange, chop-houses) and people; small attentions (saluting agreeable persons) and minute observations increase pleasure and improve the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as horticulture (nurse and manage intellectual seeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a sort of vegetable Principle in the Mind of every Man when he comes into the World; good Qualities in the Mind are lost for want of due Care in nursing and skilfully managing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education requires proper planting (right soil), manuring, necessary pruning, and artful management of early inclinations. Without such care, virtues are choked by weeds, excellent parts starved, and fruits (mature intellectual work) fail to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substantive 'fruit' over mere 'leaves' or 'flowers'
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves (words) and Flowers (fancy) are common; the desirable product is Fruit — mature, nourishing productions of Philosophy, Mathematics, close Reasoning, and handsome Argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value lasting, substantive intellectual achievements (fruit) above ornamental or transient accomplishments. While flowers and leaves have their place (amusement, taste), over-fondness for ornament is a disease; the ideal plant combines good leaves, fragrant flowers, and delicious fruit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for 'Whispers' news (newsworthiness for a gossip/whisper column)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those Pieces of News which are communicated as Secrets, and which bring a double Pleasure to the Hearer; first, as they are private History, and in the next place as they have always in them a Dash of Scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitable materials: sickness of persons in high posts; twilight visits paid and received by ministers of state; clandestine courtships and marriages; secret amours; losses at play; applications for places with successes or repulses. Use informants ('Peter Hush', 'Lady Blast') who supply timely whispers in coffee-houses; launch secrets early and let them spread through social circles for maximum effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial scope: 'Account of the Works of the Unlearned'
rubrics_metrics.description: A monthly account that reviews works by those outside learned circles — pieces in which the 'Illiterate World' makes an eminent figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include and critique works omitted by learned reviews: productions of party-authors, editors, commentators, and others often men of no learning. Consider foreign 'accounts' but focus on domestic unlearned productions; this yields ample material for satirical or critical review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ignorant or absurd similes (public speakers and writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many who speak at the Bar, Pulpit, or any publick Assembly discover their Ignorance in the Use of Similes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admonish and correct gross abuses of simile (example: comparing a person to an elephant as if it had no knees). Print warnings (e.g., in italics) to shame or reform such misuse; public speakers should be held to standards of accurate and sensible comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between true modesty and false (moral criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Modesty is ashamed to do anything repugnant to right Reason; False Modesty is ashamed to do anything that is opposite to the Humour of the Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge modesty by whether it aligns with prudence and religion (true modesty) or merely with fashion and company (false modesty). False modesty leads to indecent or imprudent compliance (lending money one cannot spare, recommending unknown people, bestowing places, living contrary to one's own judgment) and thus is culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should teach refusal (confidence to deny)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Person has had but an ill Education, who has not been taught to deny any thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate in both sexes the ability to refuse imprudent solicitations; lack of this 'confidence' (vicious modesty) betrays people into foolish or immoral actions such as drunken violence, imprudent lending, or corrupt compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercy and conduct toward the unfortunate (judging bankrupts and the fallen)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something sacred in Misery to great and good Minds; wise Lawgivers have been extremely tender how they let loose even the Man who has Right on his Side, to act with any Mixture of Resentment against the Defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid piling scorn on those made miserable by misfortune; exercise condescension and assistance rather than rejoicing at the downfall. Practical mercy: a former friend can help by appearance, accommodation of credit, or benign treatment rather than joining in reproaches; wealth carries a contagious esteem, so rich should use their influence to help formerly prosperous but fallen acquaintances.

rubrics_metrics.name: On hypocrisy vs open impiety; the due mean of religious deportment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypocrisie cannot indeed be too much detested, but at the same time is to be preferred to open Impiety... The due Mean to be observed is to be sincerely Virtuous, and at the same time to let the World see we are so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While avoiding hypocrisy, prefer at least outward appearance of devotion over blatant irreligion; the ideal is sincere virtue combined with visible practice so that religion remains present in ordinary life and conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good allegory and tasteful writing
rubrics_metrics.description: An Allegory so well carry'd on, that it cannot but be very pleasing to those who have a Taste of good Writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose allegories carefully and carry them through consistently; well-executed allegory pleases readers with taste. Use such devices to make reflections on education and morals more engaging.
